To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HYPK is a molten globule-like protein with a single tyrosyl residue situated in a helical conformation and is conformationally flexible.
HYPK is an intrinsically disordered protein that exists in a pre-molten globule state in the absence of Ca++, and that Ca++ binding causes compaction and stabilization of the protein.
the HYPK protein is intrinsically unstructu- red and has a loosely associated (molten) globule like conformation with the lone tyro- sine being situated within a helix.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biophysical characterization of HYPK, a huntingtin-interacting chaperone-like protein.
the biophysical properties of an intrinsically unfolded protein HYPK, and the role of Ca++ on its conformational flexibility.
the structural characterization of the huntingtin-interacting pro- tein HYPK.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HYPK is an IUP with an α-helical conformation.
HYPK has a conformational plasticity with an inherent ability to adopt different conforma- tions in response to different environmental factors.
HYPK is an unstructured protein in solution and in the presence of Ca++ it adopts a compact molten globule state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HYPK is an intrinsically disordered protein with an α-helical conformational propensities and that Ca++ induces compaction of this protein.
HYPK is a protein that is conformationally dynamic and can adopt a variety of conformations.
HYPK is an IUP with a conformational flexibility that can be altered by Ca++ and other factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of a chaperone, HYPK is able to adopt a (pre-)molten globule like conformation with a significant amount of residual structure.
, in vitro HYPK has a conformational flexibility and can exist in different states.

HYPK is an IUP with a conformationally flexible structure and the protein can be considered a chaperone-like protein in the sense that it has a (pre-)molten globule structure with an ability to undergo conformational changes.
